shared cause (e.g., a cloud provider outage) is often a deliberately chosen, economically motivated shared dependency.","Trees cannot actively choose to diversify their root systems to avoid drought, whereas independent service operators could theoretically choose diverse infrastructure but often do not due to economic incentives."],"overturn_conditions":["Evidence that a single large service can effectively isolate its internal redundancy against shared causes better than decentralized nodes can isolate themselves from each other.","Proof that decentralized operators, despite lacking a central authority, naturally diverge in their infrastructure choices enough to prevent correlated failures without enforcement."],"shared_structure":["Both involve a collection of locally independent units (distributed services vs. individual trees) that appear uncorrelated but can succumb to a single shared environmental shock (shared cloud infrastructure vs. regional drought).","Resilience in both cases is determined not by the count or redundancy of individual units, but by the diversity of their underlying dependencies (vendor heterogeneity vs. species/genetic diversity)."],"source_memory_refs":["c1fadd936d722e21db6970d43b969e25df9f1478f1b8bc5f1716fecc780a4d0e"],"transfer_claims":["Just as a genetically uniform forest is resilient to local pests but wiped out by a species-specific disease, a decentralized network running identical software stacks is resilient to operator error but wiped out by a shared software vulnerability.","The empirical test for While a large service might have N internal redundant components, they are typically subject to a unified control plane and identical vendor stack. Decentralized services achieve true resilience only if their independent operation prevents the propagation of correlated shocks (e.g., shared cloud outages, CDN failures, or zero-day vulnerabilities in shared dependencies).
